columns.heading: What Winning Lineups Usually Got Right
columns.body: In a completed fantasy week, the biggest edge usually came from backing players who could turn match wins into layered scoring. The strongest builds typically combined advancement with repeatable point sources such as aces, hold stability, and efficient wins instead of relying only on one upset to carry the roster.
bullets: Deep-run equity matters most when it also brings steady scoring peripherals.
Bonus Ball usually pays off best when attached to both ceiling and match-volume safety.
Balanced builds tend to outperform when mid-tier players convert clean paths into multiple useful rounds.
Completed slates often reward process over hype: route quality and scoring profile usually beat name value alone.

columns.heading: What Likely Hurt Rosters
columns.body: The most common misses in a finished week usually come from overpaying for fragile paths, chasing volatile underdogs, or using the multiplier on a player whose route was less stable than it looked. Results editions are about identifying those roster leaks and tightening the process for next time.
bullets: Premium salary without a deep run often becomes the fastest way to lose lineup ground.
Cheap value that exits early rarely recovers unless it lands a major upset bonus first.
Bonus Ball misses are especially costly when safer high-volume options were available.
One flashy result does not erase a weak overall roster structure if the rest of the lineup stalls early.

cards.title: What Matters Most From The Week 2939 Results
paragraphs: ATP Fantasy still revolves around the same core structure: 100 credits, six starters, two alternates, and one Bonus Ball player scoring double. In a results edition, the main job is to study what the completed week usually rewards: players who stayed alive long enough to stack points, servers who kept producing even in tighter matches, and lineups that avoided dead spots from fragile value or early premium exits.

Because the primary ATP current scores, live rankings, results archive, news, and official tournament detail packets were unavailable in this cycle, this review remains intentionally conservative on player-specific outcomes, tournament naming, and exact result claims. The clearest customer-facing takeaway is structural: completed ATP Fantasy weeks are usually won by combining advancement, efficient wins, and portable scoring traits rather than by chasing volatility across too many roster spots.
cards.subtitle: Results Edition Themes
bullets: Finished slates usually reward players who combine wins with repeatable scoring.
Bonus Ball outcomes often decide whether a good lineup becomes a great one.
Mid-tier outperformers can swing the week when they turn manageable paths into multiple wins.
Early exits from expensive roster spots are usually the biggest drag on final score.

items.body: Lineups generally score best when they spread exposure across players with realistic multi-round paths instead of forcing too many boom-or-bust picks into the same build.
Aces, hold strength, and efficient wins remain the cleanest way to build dependable fantasy totals over a completed week.
The strongest post-week review is to identify which picks had both route quality and scoring portability, then carry that filter forward.
If a player needed several low-probability events to pay off, the profile was probably too fragile for a core roster spot from the start.

cards.title: Top Performer Archetypes From A Completed Week

items.body: The best expensive plays are usually the ones that justified salary with both advancement and a scoring base strong enough to keep producing through multiple rounds.
The biggest value swings often come from mid-range players who turn a manageable section into two or more useful wins.
When part of the bracket opens up, the fantasy winner is often the player who actually converts that opening instead of merely looking attractive on paper.
Players who generate steady ace volume and protect serve well often remain useful even when the path is not completely soft.
The multiplier tends to hit best on players who paired route safety with enough upside to stack points across several matches.
An aggressive Bonus Ball can work when a high-ceiling scorer also gets enough runway to build momentum early in the week.
Bonus Ball choices usually disappoint when they depend on surviving immediate danger rather than controlling matches.
If two candidates look close, the better multiplier target is usually the one more likely to win efficiently and stay on court longer in the tournament.
The strongest low-cost performers usually brought at least one bankable fantasy trait, such as ace production or upset capability, and then stayed alive long enough to matter.
Useful bargains often emerge when a mid or lower-tier player gets a realistic path to one or two wins instead of needing a miracle run.
Alternates are most useful when they come from sections you genuinely trust, not just from the cheapest names available.
A punt generally needs both survival odds and one repeatable scoring trait to become a real fantasy asset over a full week.

cards.title: Misses, Traps, And What They Mean Next

items.body: Even strong players can underdeliver when their route asks for too many difficult wins too early in the event.
Cheap names often fail when salary relief is the only argument and the path offers little real scoring runway.
Reputation alone is rarely enough if the salary assumes a deep run that the bracket or form does not support.
Use the completed week to tighten your pool around players whose scoring profile can survive both favorable and moderately difficult matchups.
